source.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
source.authors: Zhaofeng Wu; Xinyan Velocity Yu; Dani Yogatama; Jia-Sen Lu; Yoon Kim

record.file_problem: Minor OCR and encoding artifacts; the full paper and appendices are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether semantically paired inputs have more similar representations using layerwise similarity measures, but does not test cross-model alignment or its increase with model scale and capability.
record.gate_note: The study measures representation similarity for paired inputs within individual models, including image-caption pairs. It does not measure alignment between independently trained models or whether such alignment rises with size or performance. Logit-lens anchoring analyses and deliberate steering interventions do not measure the claim's cross-model convergence trend; those results are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether semantically paired inputs, such as translations, image-caption pairs and audio-label pairs, get similar hidden states inside one jointly trained model. It does not compare representations across independently trained models, seeds or modalities' separate encoders, and it has no size or capability trend. The authors call their work 'complementary and distinct' from cross-model alignment work such as the PRH. None of V1–V7 names this construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that LMs represent semantically similar inputs from different languages and modalities near one another in intermediate layers. They also find this space is interpretable through the dominant language, and that intervening in it through that language predictably changes outputs.
record.recipe_differences: Measures similarity between different input types within a single multilingual or multimodal model, rather than alignment between independently trained models or alignment as models scale.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer and input type vary: translation similarities are strongest in intermediate layers, and the arithmetic similarity advantage decreases toward zero in later layers. The study does not compare alternative similarity metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: Within jointly trained VLMs (LLaVA-7B, Chameleon-7B), matching image-caption pairs have higher intermediate-layer cosine similarity than non-matching pairs. The authors say this emerges without an explicit contrastive objective.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single multimodal model trained on images and text represents paired image and caption inputs more similarly than unpaired ones in intermediate layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Within LMs, translations, equivalent arithmetic expressions, sentence and semantic-structure pairs, and audio-label pairs are more similar than non-matching pairs. BLOOM is near chance on formal semantics, which the authors tentatively link to model capacity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language models share an intermediate semantic hub across languages and modalities.

record.problems: The study does not measure whether cross-model alignment increases with size or capability, and does not test separately trained vision and language models. Several reported similarity values are available only in plots. The authors also note that BLOOM is not much better than chance on the formal-semantics experiment.
record.rows_left_out: Logit-lens anchoring results for languages, arithmetic, code, semantic roles, image patches, and audio labels were not included because they measure hidden-state-to-token correspondence rather than pairwise representation similarity for the cataloged versions. The section 4 steering results were omitted because the behavior is deliberately induced and the outcome is not a measure of representation alignment.

untested.parts: All: no cross-model comparison, no scale or capability trend.
All: no separately trained vision and language models, and no trend with model quality. Only within-model image-caption similarity in two single VLMs.
All: no mapping or stitching between models.
All: no cross-model feature or circuit recurrence.
All: only cosine similarity is used, and no alternative metrics are compared.
All: no cross-model alignment levels or causes are examined.

record.verdict_notes: No version linked, so no verdicts. The capacity remark about BLOOM is a within-model speculation, not a cross-model convergence-with-scale result. The reader's 'partial' states for the controls in Llama-2, Llama-3 and Baichuan-2 contradict the text, which reports the same trend holding.

versions.untested_parts: Whether representations of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data become more aligned as models grow and become more capable.
Whether alignment increases as the vision and language models improve; alignment between separately trained vision and language models.
Convergence across random initialization seeds, including shared features or subspaces.
Mapping or stitching representations between models, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Whether convergence changes under alternative similarity metrics, metric settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Whether alignment is incomplete or plateaus, or whether shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality explain it.

rows.subject: LLaVA-7B

rows.measure: Cosine similarity increase over the nonmatching-pair baseline
rows.uncertainty: 95% CI plotted; numeric values not stated
rows.note: The authors report that matching cross-modal inputs are more similar than nonmatching pairs.
rows.check: Within-model image-caption similarity in a single jointly trained VLM (LLaVA-7B). V2 concerns alignment between vision and language models' representations as both improve. The kind of system differs and no improvement trend is measured, so this does not bear on V2.
